tip: The 'ke-...-an' pattern marks accidents: 'tinggal' = stay behind, 'ketinggalan' = got left behind – nobody did it on purpose. Same move in 'ketiduran' (accidentally fell asleep).
'Boarding pass' stays English at Indonesian airports; 'pintu' = gate here.
The '-an' ending turns an action into its thing: 'antre' = to queue up, 'antrean' = the line itself. Same trick in 'makan' – 'makanan' (food), 'minum' – 'minuman' (drink).
The 'di-' prefix flips who does it: 'menunda' = postpone, 'ditunda' = postponed; 'penerbangan ditunda' = the flight is delayed.
'Baru' means new, but before a verb it means only just or not until: 'penerbangan pengganti baru ada besok' = the replacement flight isn't there until tomorrow.
English says you missed the plane; Indonesian says the plane left you behind: 'ketinggalan pesawat' = got left behind by the plane.
'AC' (said ah-seh) = air conditioning; 'rusak' = broken: 'AC di kamar kami rusak' = the AC in our room is broken.
'Sampai' usually means until, but after a description it means so much that: 'berisik sekali sampai kami tidak bisa tidur' = so noisy we couldn't sleep.
'Mampet' = clogged, the everyday word; 'tersumbat' is what a plumber's report says.
'Keluarnya kecil' = its flow is weak: '-nya' turns 'keluar' (come out) into a noun, the coming-out.
'Belum' = not yet, the negative for anything still pending: 'belum ada yang datang' = no one has come yet. 'Tidak' would state it flatly, as if no one will.
Adding '-nya' to a whole phrase marks it as the one already discussed: 'masalah air panasnya' = that hot-water problem.
'SIM' = driving licence, short for 'Surat Izin Mengemudi'; it's said as one word (seem).
Stick '-an' on a time word to make it recurring: 'hari' – 'harian' (daily), 'minggu' – 'mingguan' (weekly), 'bulan' – 'bulanan' (monthly), so 'sewa harian' = daily rental.
'Seluruh' = the whole of one thing: 'seluruh keluarga' = the whole family; 'semua keluarga' = all the (separate) families.
'Pulang pergi' is literally go-home go – the trip home gets named first. 'Tiket pulang pergi' = a round-trip ticket, often shortened to 'PP' on booking sites.
The everyday way to say per is 'se-' (one): 'dua kali sehari' = twice a day, literally two times one-day.
'Salah' slots before almost any verb to mean doing it wrong: 'salah beli' = bought the wrong one, 'salah paham' = misunderstood, 'salah sambung' = dialed the wrong number.
'Numpang tanya' is a set phrase to stop a stranger politely, like excuse me, may I ask.
'Pak' or 'Bu' before a question keeps it polite: 'maaf, Pak' = excuse me, sir.
'Maaf sudah merepotkan' = sorry for the trouble – a polite closer after someone helps.
'Kalau boleh tahu' = if I may ask – it softens personal questions.
'Sama' normally means same, but in everyday speech it also means with: 'sama keluarga' = with family. 'Dengan' is the formal version.
'Syukuran' = a small thanksgiving do for good news; 'syukuran rumah baru' = a housewarming.
'Datang ke' + event or place = come to: 'datang ke ulang tahun' = come to the birthday. The 'ke' normally stays.
'Jadi' before a verb checks a plan still holds: 'kamu jadi datang?' = are you still coming?
'Mengajak' = casually ask someone along; 'mengundang' = properly invite. 'Dia mengajak kami makan' = she asked us to eat.
'Arisan' = a savings-and-social gathering, usually monthly; members pool money and one takes the pot.
After a negative, 'apa-apa' = anything: 'tidak perlu bawa apa-apa' = no need to bring anything.
'Nikahan' is the everyday word for a wedding; 'pernikahan' is the formal one on invitations.
